clinicalPearls: A malignant pleural effusion indicates disseminated or advanced malignancy and generally portends a poor prognosis.
Lung and breast carcinoma account for the majority; lymphoma, ovarian and gastric cancers and mesothelioma are other important causes, and a proportion arise from an unknown primary.

Effusions are typically exudative by Light's criteria and are frequently blood-stained; a massive effusion with mediastinal shift towards the effusion suggests a central obstructing tumour or mesothelioma.
Low pleural fluid pH and glucose correlate with higher tumour burden, poorer pleurodesis success and shorter survival.
Pleural fluid cytology confirms malignancy in only around 60 percent of cases, with sensitivity higher in adenocarcinoma and low in mesothelioma.
When cytology is negative, image-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy provides tissue for diagnosis and molecular characterisation.
Definitive management aims at symptom control through therapeutic aspiration, talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter, guided by patient preference and the presence of trapped lung.
Prognostic scores such as LENT and PROMISE help select the least burdensome yet most durable management strategy.
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant effusions form when tumour involves the pleura, most often through haematogenous or lymphatic metastasis to the parietal and visceral pleura or by direct invasion. Pleural tumour increases capillary and mesothelial permeability, elaborates vascular endothelial growth factor and other mediators, and obstructs the lymphatic stomata and mediastinal lymphatics that normally drain the pleural space. The combination of increased fluid formation and impaired lymphatic reabsorption produces a progressive exudate. Extensive visceral pleural tumour or fibrosis may prevent the lung re-expanding after drainage (trapped lung), which strongly influences the choice between pleurodesis and an indwelling catheter.
additionalDifferentials: Transudative effusion from heart failure or hepatic hydrothorax
Paramalignant effusion from lymphatic obstruction or post-obstructive pneumonia rather than direct pleural involvement
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic pleural aspiration with cytology, protein, LDH, pH and glucose
Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax with abdomen and pelvis for staging
Thoracic ultrasound to assess pleural nodularity, septations and guide sampling
Image-guided or local anaesthetic thoracoscopic pleural biopsy
Immunohistochemistry and molecular studies on pleural tissue or fluid
Assessment of lung re-expansion after drainage to detect trapped lung
Prognostic scoring (LENT or PROMISE) alongside performance status assessment
redFlags: Rapid re-accumulation with breathlessness at rest
Massive effusion with contralateral mediastinal shift
Ipsilateral or absent mediastinal shift suggesting trapped lung or central airway obstruction
Features of superior vena cava obstruction
Signs of pleural infection complicating an indwelling catheter
reference.prognosis: Survival is generally measured in months and varies markedly with tumour type and fluid characteristics, being worse with low pleural fluid pH or glucose and poor performance status; mesothelioma and lung primaries carry the poorest outlook, whereas breast cancer and haematological malignancies may respond to systemic therapy.
pitfalls: Relying on a single negative cytology to exclude malignancy.
Attempting pleurodesis in a trapped lung, which is likely to fail.
Draining a large effusion too rapidly and precipitating re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Mislabelling a paramalignant effusion, which may respond to systemic therapy, as directly malignant.
Not offering an indwelling pleural catheter to patients with limited prognosis or a non-expandable lung.
references: ERS/EACTS Statement on the Management of Malignant Pleural Effusions
management: Direct treatment at the underlying malignancy with systemic chemotherapy, targeted or hormonal therapy according to tumour type, which may control fluid reaccumulation
Therapeutic pleural aspiration to relieve breathlessness, with the volume drained guided by symptoms
Chemical pleurodesis, typically with talc, for recurrent effusion when the lung re-expands fully after drainage
Indwelling pleural catheter for trapped lung, failed pleurodesis or patient preference, allowing ambulatory drainage
Assess lung re-expansion after drainage to choose between pleurodesis and an indwelling catheter
Symptomatic relief of breathlessness with opioids and other measures alongside early palliative care involvement
Manage through a multidisciplinary team of respiratory medicine, oncology and palliative care
